newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRENCH WHEAT YIELDS CONVERGE AFTER WIDE 1996 GAP.
newsitem.headline: FRENCH WHEAT YIELDS CONVERGE AFTER WIDE 1996 GAP.

text.p: France's main bread-basket region south of Paris is recovering from last year's disappointing wheat yields, the farm ministry said on Tuesday.
But the north, where outstanding yields helped to deliver France's biggest wheat crop in 1996, will be less productive this time, the ministry forecast in an August crop report.
Overall, it expects France to produce 33.2 million tonnes of soft wheat in 1997, second only to last year's 34.7 million.
National yields have fallen to an estimated 6.84 tonnes per hectare from last year's 7.27 tonnes, also a record.
The ministry's latest figures show that farmers partially compensated for this by sowing an extra 1.8 percent of land to soft wheat as the European Union eased set-aside restrictions.
Soft wheat sowings rose to 4.858 million hectares this year from last year's 4.77 million.
But the trend in intensive European yields is still rising.
This year's national yield of 6.84 tonnes per hectare is above the 6.6 tonnes seen in 1995, the ministry said.
According to other data from the ONIC grain authority, the ministry's 1997 yield forecast is 2.5 percent higher than ONIC's five-year yield average of 6.67 tonnes for 1991 to 1995.
The ministry's report suggested yields in individual regions would converge somewhat this year after last year's extremes.

Last year the bread-basket Centre region, the biggest by volume in France, failed to pick up on strong yields seen elsewhere due to a drought. But farmers north of the river Seine cashed in on a late break in dry weather.

Based around Orleans, the Centre produced a below-average 6.4 tonnes per hectare while the Nord Pas-de-Calais region near Lille in the north produced a record 10.2 tonnes, 30 percent above average, according to ONIC.

This year, the ministry says both Centre and Ile-de-France, which includes Paris, will see their soft wheat yields rebound by by 0.4 tonnes per hectare. Burgundy in the east, whose capital is Dijon, will gain 0.2 tonnes per hectare.
The main loser is Nord-Pas de Calais, down by "more than 1.5 tonnes per hectare," and yields in the Lorraine region near Nancy will lose about one tonne, the ministry said.

France's second wheat producing region of Picardie near Amiens will give up 0.7 tonnes per hectare while third-ranked Champagne-Ardennes, whose figures are recorded under Chalons-sur-Marne, expects a decrease of 0.3 tonnes.

The ministry's figures are based on information available on August 1. Since then the harvest has paused north of Paris for heavy rain last week. Apart from some waterlogged areas in the northeast most harvesting resumed in sunshine at the weekend.
